findings.description: The schema reformat carried one real tightening: per_id entries are now checked against $defs.entry. Nothing checked that the code writing per_id obeys that entry shape, and it does not — the bug-hunt branch reuses `state` to carry a witness status, whose spelling was never in the state vocabulary. The tool's own test suite exercises no bug-hunt grade, so the gate is green while the verb is broken. Either the enum must admit the witness statuses (they are a different axis and probably want their own key) or line 274 must map them onto the state vocabulary; the tightening itself is right and should stay.
findings.why_it_matters: `Passes.grade` line 274 writes `entry["state"] = r === nothing ? nothing : uppercase(String(r.status))` from a re-run witness, and `Witnesses.WitnessResult.status` is `:pass`, `:fail`, `:broken` or `:blocked` — so `state` becomes "PASS"/"FAIL"/"BROKEN"/"BLOCKED". The tightened `$defs.entry.state` enum is `PRESENT | PARTIAL | REGRESSED | ABSENT | NOT-A-DEFECT | UNCLEAR | null`. At base `per_id` was unvalidated (`additionalProperties: true`, no items), so any entry passed; at head line 318's `validate(load_schema("tally"), tally)` fails and `grade` throws `RoundError`, caught at Rounds.jl:668 as exit 2. This is the NORMAL success path of a bug-hunt round: a finding whose reproduction disposition is `fixed` and whose witness now passes. Ran it: with per_id entry {act: null, act_demoted: false, state: "PASS", closed_by: "honored"} and every other tally key as grade builds it, the BASE schema VALIDATES and the HEAD schema REFUSES with `$.per_id.<id>.state: "PASS" is not one of "PRESENT", "PARTIAL", "REGRESSED", "ABSENT", "NOT-A-DEFECT", "UNCLEAR", nothing`. No bug-hunt round can be graded past its first fixed finding.

findings.description: Aligning the schema with CFG.EXEMPTIONS is defensible, but it changes the failure MODE of previously-loadable input from a graded finding to an unhandled exception, and it does so for the four consumers' existing ledgers, none of which were migrated in this commit and none of which the diff inspects. If the alignment is wanted, either the callers must catch LedgerError and degrade to an empty ledger the way Doctor.context does, or the migration must come first.
findings.why_it_matters: The base description records the loose bound as deliberate: the schema stayed at 24 so that CFG.EXEMPTIONS could REPORT the 40-character rule as a doctor FAIL (exit 1, a finding) instead of the loader refusing to load. `Ledger.read` (Ledger.jl:38) throws `LedgerError` on any schema error, and it is the default keyword of `Sync.sync`, `Sync.plan`, `Sync.status`, `Sync.slots` and `Scan.run_scan`, none of which catch it; `main` catches everything and returns 3 (`crashed`). Only `Doctor.context` catches it. Ran it on an otherwise valid entry with a 30-character reason: BASE VALIDATES, HEAD refuses with `$.exemption[1].reason: shorter than 40 characters`. So a consumer whose ledger the doctor merely marked red now cannot run `gbg sync`, `gbg scan docs`, or a docs build (the makedocs wrapper runs the hard scans, which read the ledger).

findings.description: This diff adds a concrete, actionable `--glob '!.gbg/**'` grep-scoping instruction to two workflow scripts (RULE.DOC.CLASS_SWEEP: "a flagged instance is a sample of a class; fix the class, not the line") but the class — every workflow script that grants broad tree-read access adjacent to `.gbg/` round data — has at least four other members, two of which (dismissals.js, audit.js) were touched in this identical diff for unrelated reasons and left with the older, weaker wording.
findings.after: hunt.js (head): "Nothing under `.gbg/` or `~/.gbg/` is yours to open but the files this prompt names; scope every grep with `--glob '!.gbg/**'`."; panel.js (head) adds the identical "scope every search with `--glob '!.gbg/**'`" to its git/grep grant. Every other workflow script that grants the same broad Bash/Read access over the repo tree — including two others touched in this very diff (dismissals.js, audit.js) — still reads only the older, weaker prohibition: dismissals.js:38 "Read the CURRENT tree at ${A.repo} (nothing else under .gbg/, never ~/.gbg/)"; audit.js:71 "FILES UNDER .gbg/ YOU MAY OPEN — exactly these, with Read, and nothing else under .gbg/ or ~/.gbg/" (a bare list + prohibition, no grep-scoping technique).
findings.before: hunt.js (base): "Read the source. Follow the data. Ask, of each thing you read, what would have to be true for it to be correct, and then check whether it is." — no grep-scoping guidance anywhere in the sibling scripts either.
findings.why_it_matters: These scripts hand an agent with live Grep/Bash access instructions to read "the current tree"/"the source" broadly right next to a `.gbg/rounds/` tree that holds prior rounds' verdicts and findings — an answer key for the very task being re-run. The fix in hunt.js/panel.js exists because a bare textual prohibition is not enough for an agent wielding an unscoped `grep -r`: a single broad search silently sweeps in `.gbg/` content. This is not hypothetical — running this exact audit, a broad `grep -rn "caveats" .` (no `--glob` exclusion) surfaced verbatim excerpts from `.gbg/rounds/2026-09-09-check-docs-02/verdicts/*.json`, i.e. a prior round's answer key for the identical HOME_ORDER question this diff touches. audit.js and dismissals.js grant an agent the same unscoped power and were edited in this same diff without picking up the mitigation their sibling files received.

findings.description: The diff builds the first mechanical enforcer for a rule whose text (left untouched, so it is the honest baseline of what the package promises) names three exemptions; the enforcer implements only two of them. This is exactly the shape of a check shipped without checking it against its own rule's stated exceptions — the kind of gap RULE.TEST.RULE_WITH_CHECK's self-application sweep (also new in this diff) was meant to surface, but the sweep only verifies that a `check` field exists, not that the check matches the rule's text.
findings.after: This diff adds the rule's first-ever enforcer, SCAN.ARGS_FORM ('new 2026-09-09' per the scans table), whose implementation only recognises two exemptions: `startswith(d.binding, "_")` and `occursin(Reflection.WRAPPER_PHRASE, d.body)` (plus a fields-list skip). Its logic is `wants_bullets = length(pos) + length(kw) >= Reflection.ARGS_THRESHOLD || !isempty(kw)` — ANY keyword argument, including the exact case the rubric calls out ("a single element-type keyword bound in one prose clause"), now forces the bulleted form and is flagged `wrong-args-form` if written in prose.
findings.before: RULE.DOC.ARGS_FORM has stood since before this diff (untouched by it) reading: "Exempt: a thin allocating wrapper, which documents no arguments at all; an internal `_`-prefixed helper, which documents its arguments in whatever form reads best; and a single element-type keyword bound in one prose clause." No scan or doctor check enforced this rule at base — a reader could rely on the written exemptions with no machine second-guessing them.
findings.why_it_matters: A reader of docs-rubric.md — the rubric this package renders into every consumer's CLAUDE.md — is told a single element-type keyword documented in running prose is fine. The newly-built scan disagrees and will flag it in every fleet package the moment `check-docs` runs there, with no ledger entry or rubric footnote explaining the gap. Because the scan is triage tier it won't fail a round outright, but it manufactures a finding a reviewer must then dismiss every time the documented exemption is exercised, and a first-time reader has no way to know the written rule and the running tool disagree.
findings.title: New SCAN.ARGS_FORM enforces a narrower exemption set than the standing RULE.DOC.ARGS_FORM promise
findings.evidence: policy/docs-rubric.md: "a single element-type keyword bound in one prose clause" (exempt) vs src/Scans/args_form.jl: "wants_bullets = length(pos) + length(kw) >= Reflection.ARGS_THRESHOLD || !isempty(kw)" with no exemption path for a lone keyword.
